did_you_know.text: The chapter opens by introducing Ecclesiastes as the “son of David” and king in Jerusalem, but his personal name is not mentioned in the verse.
The phrase “Vanity of vanities” emphasizes the idea of futility, and it returns later in the chapter as an introduction to Ecclesiastes’ conclusion about human existence.
Ecclesiastes raises a central question: What advantage or gain does a person have from all their labor “under the sun”?
The verse contrasts the passing generations—“A generation goes and a generation comes”—with the earth, which is described as enduring forever.
The movement of the sun is described as cyclical: it rises, sets, and returns to its place to rise again.
Ecclesiastes describes the water cycle: the rivers flow into the sea, yet the sea is not filled, and the waters return to the places from which they will flow again.
According to Ecclesiastes, what appears to be new has already existed in the past; therefore, he declares that there is nothing new under the sun.
The chapter emphasizes the fleeting nature of memory: no complete remembrance of earlier generations is preserved, and future generations will also be forgotten.
Ecclesiastes points to the limits of human ability: wrongs that remain uncorrected and deficiencies that cannot be counted are not solved simply through effort.
The chapter ends by stating that as a person gains more wisdom and knowledge, anger and sorrow may also increase.
